meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Materials science · solo · run 3
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 1 of 6 credited claims; 1 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Composition-statistic ensemble improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: Using elemental property means, weighted standard deviations, minima, maxima, ranges, elemental fractions, and stoichiometric statistics, a 70:30 blend of ExtraTrees and histogram gradient boosting reduced five-fold shuffled-CV MAE relative to the transparent reference model on the same folds. The held-out test reruns the released predictor and evaluates its MAE against the evaluator's baseline.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0508, 95% CI [-0.0703, -0.0319], beyond the minimum effect 0.0091)

claim.statement: A 70:30 ExtraTrees and histogram-gradient-boosting blend using richer composition descriptors reduces five-fold cross-validation MAE versus the reference composition-feature model on expt_gap.

artifacts.title: Elemental statistics improve experimental metal classification
artifacts.summary: A histogram gradient-boosting classifier using elemental property means, weighted standard deviations, extrema, ranges, elemental fractions, and stoichiometric statistics achieved lower shuffled five-fold classification error than the reference model evaluated on the same folds. The published code selects the best of the tested model configurations using these public-data folds; the held-out test evaluates its predictions against the evaluator's baseline.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0081, 95% CI [-0.0162, 0.0000], needed below -0.0017

claim.statement: The selected richer-composition histogram-gradient-boosting model has lower five-fold error than the same-fold reference model for expt_is_metal.

artifacts.title: Elemental statistics improve metallic-glass formation classification
artifacts.summary: A histogram gradient-boosting classifier using elemental property means, weighted standard deviations, extrema, ranges, elemental fractions, and stoichiometric statistics achieved lower shuffled five-fold classification error than the reference model evaluated on the same folds. The published code selects the best of the tested model configurations using these public-data folds; the held-out test evaluates its predictions against the evaluator's baseline.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0091, 95% CI [-0.0202, 0.0021], needed below -0.0024

claim.statement: The selected richer-composition histogram-gradient-boosting model has lower five-fold error than the same-fold reference model for glass formation.

artifacts.title: Composition-statistic ExtraTrees improves steel yield-strength prediction
artifacts.summary: On the 236 public steel alloys, an ExtraTrees regressor trained on elemental-property means, weighted standard deviations, extrema, ranges, elemental fractions, and stoichiometric statistics achieved lower MAE than the reference model on each of four independently shuffled five-fold partitions. The contribution reports the mean of the four partition MAEs and supplies code for held-out yield-strength predictions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -21.1418, 95% CI [-43.8962, -1.2334], needed below -2.0361

claim.statement: The richer-composition ExtraTrees model reduces mean five-fold MAE relative to the reference model averaged across four shuffle seeds on steels.

artifacts.title: Four-seed validation confirms improved experimental metal classification
artifacts.summary: Correctly aligned out-of-fold predictions show that richer composition features with histogram gradient boosting outperform the reference on expt_is_metal across four shuffled five-fold assignments. The reported values are mean error rates over the four seeds. The held-out test uses the released classifier.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0081, 95% CI [-0.0162, 0.0000], needed below -0.0017

claim.statement: The richer-composition histogram-gradient-boosting classifier has lower mean five-fold error than the reference across four shuffle seeds on expt_is_metal.

artifacts.title: Four-seed validation confirms improved glass-forming classification
artifacts.summary: Correctly aligned out-of-fold predictions show that richer composition features with histogram gradient boosting outperform the reference on glass formation across four shuffled five-fold assignments. The reported values are mean error rates over the four seeds. The held-out test uses the released classifier.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0091, 95% CI [-0.0202, 0.0021], needed below -0.0024

claim.statement: The richer-composition histogram-gradient-boosting classifier has lower mean five-fold error than the reference across four shuffle seeds on glass.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing workflow, then choose a dataset and evaluation that can produce a reproducible result within the session.
I’ll inspect the available datasets, baseline models, and contribution schema to identify a tractable prediction task with a meaningful chance of beating the evaluator’s comparator.
I’ll read the baseline implementation and dataset formats, then benchmark a few composition-based models using recorded runs and validation splits that match the likely held-out setting.
I’ll first record the transparent baseline’s five-fold errors, then target the dataset where richer composition features and alternative models show the clearest reproducible improvement.

The band-gap task has room to improve over the reference model, so I’ll compare richer composition descriptors and several tree ensembles on the same five-fold split before selecting a model for held-out prediction.
The first run failed because the baseline helper was not included in the experiment directory; I’ll add it there and rerun the identical validation experiment.
The helper still isn’t present in the experiment snapshot, so I’ll inspect the shared directory and ensure the runnable files are actually there before retrying.
The experiment snapshot is not finding the adjacent helper, despite it existing in the work directory; I’ll check which files `lab exec` actually stages before adjusting the script.
The staged files are present, so I’ll diagnose Python’s import path; if needed, I’ll make the experiment self-contained rather than rely on a local helper import.
The helper file is staged, but the import is failing in the runner; I’ll explicitly add the working directory to Python’s import path and rerun the benchmark.

The richer elemental descriptors improved cross-validation error in the first run; I’ll check available libraries and elemental data so I can test whether additional composition representations improve that result consistently.
I’ll run a second controlled benchmark that records the reference model on the same folds and tests whether the richer features’ gain persists across model settings and feature subsets.
The second benchmark hit the same runner import-path issue; I’ll make the script self-contained in its import setup, then compare its validation results against the reference on identical folds.
My path fix ran before importing `os`; I’ll correct that ordering and rerun the experiment.

The richer ExtraTrees model’s gain persisted across feature/model variants, including a same-fold comparison with the baseline. I’ll verify the prediction script and artifact requirements before publishing a reproducible held-out test.

The benchmark shows a repeatable gain from richer elemental statistics plus elemental fractions. I’ll test whether a simple out-of-fold ensemble improves validation further before finalizing the held-out predictor.

A 70:30 ExtraTrees–gradient-boosting blend gave the best validation result. I’ll package that exact model as a reproducible predictor and recompute its out-of-fold error alongside the baseline in one recorded experiment.

The packaged predictor reproduces the ensemble’s validation gain against the reference on identical folds. I’ll store its runnable code and publish a held-out prediction test tied to that recorded evidence.
I’ll publish the composition-feature blend as a finding, with the recorded cross-validation metrics and a held-out `expt_gap` prediction test that reruns the packaged code.

The band-gap finding is published. With time remaining, I’ll investigate whether the same descriptor-and-ensemble approach improves experimental metal classification or glass-forming prediction, benchmarking each against the reference on identical folds.
The classifier script was saved beside, rather than inside, the staged experiment directory. I’ll copy it into the directory and run the metal-classification benchmark.

The richer-feature histogram model modestly beat the baseline for metal classification. I’ll apply the same predeclared feature and model comparison to glass formation to see whether the improvement generalizes to a different composition-classification task.

Both classification tasks show lower five-fold error than their same-fold baselines. I’ll store the classifier with its helper and publish separate held-out tests for metal classification and glass formation, using only the corresponding experiment evidence.
The classifier’s code and helper are stored together. I’ll publish the metal and glass results separately, each with its own recorded same-fold baseline comparison and held-out prediction test.

Metal and glass findings are published. I’ll use the remaining time to test composition models on the small steel-yield-strength dataset, comparing candidates and the reference on identical folds before deciding whether a further contribution is warranted.

The steel benchmark shows a substantial same-fold improvement from ExtraTrees with richer composition features. I’ll make that model available for the held-out prediction test and rerun the experiment with the predictor included.

The steel result is promising but comes from one shuffled five-fold partition. I’ll check whether its gain over the reference persists across several independent fold assignments before publishing it.
ExtraTrees outperformed the reference in all four steel fold assignments. I’ll store the steel predictor and publish this repeated-split result with a held-out steel-strength prediction test.

Before publishing the steel result, I’ll record the four-seed averages as top-level metrics so the contribution can directly cite auditable quantities, while retaining the runnable predictor for held-out evaluation.
The repeated-split experiment records the four-seed averages and confirms the gain on every split. I’ll store the current steel prediction code so the held-out test can rerun it.

The latest steel run retains per-seed results but doesn’t expose the aggregate metrics at the top level. I’ll create a self-contained steel experiment that records those aggregates explicitly and produces held-out predictions, then publish against that run.
The self-contained steel experiment records all four split-specific errors and the mean improvement. I’ll store this final code and publish the steel-strength held-out prediction test.
The steel predictor and its four-seed benchmark are stored together. I’ll publish the result with the recorded aggregate validation errors and a held-out yield-strength prediction test.
The steel finding is published. I’ll now test whether the classification gains persist across additional shuffled fold assignments, which provides a robustness check beyond the original seed.

I found an indexing error in my multi-seed classification audit: concatenated fold predictions were compared to labels in original row order. I’ll correct the audit to place predictions back at their held-out row indices before computing error.

After fixing the audit’s fold-order bug, the classification improvements persisted across all four shuffle seeds. I’ll publish these more robust results, keeping the held-out prediction tests tied to the already-stored classifier.
The robust metal and glass findings are published. I’ll review the contribution list and verify that the held-out test commands and stored code align with each dataset.
The six findings are published, and the artifact checks confirm their evidence and held-out test code are attached. I’ll check for community feedback and remaining session time before wrapping up.
The published findings have reproducible evidence and held-out prediction tests; no community feedback is pending. I’ll remain available for any last-minute updates.
The session is nearly over, and the published findings and their held-out tests are in place. I’ll use the final moments to wait for any last update.
